title: Knowledge Check 5: Lessons 21-25
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 21-25 of the hermes-consultant-intermediate series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson about the real agent engagement case study, what is the central focus?
options: One agent engagement from first call to handover, told in sequence with the mistakes left in, to teach sequencing over techniques
A review of unrelated sales tools
A history of the ERP vendor
A summary of procurement policy
questions.explanation: The lesson runs twenty techniques together in sequence because the sequence is the part no single technique lesson can teach.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Absorb the duplicate-SKU cleanup into the engagement because you are in the data anyway
Name a client defect with evidence and refuse to own it, pricing around it instead of absorbing it
Keep silent to the sponsor about the Tuesday the export changed
Decline the follow-on order entry work without explaining why
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that rolling the cleanup in would cost unpaid days, make exclusions soft, and hide a data governance problem, so you name the defect and refuse to own it.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A handover is written on the last day so it describes the final system
Measurement is defined after the change so it fits the result
Design for a loud failure that stops rather than producing plausible output from unexpected input
The golden set is graded by the delivered system itself
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the most valuable build decision is that the pipeline stops rather than produces plausible output, so failures are loud and diagnosable.

questions.question: Per the lesson about building repeatable processes, what is the central focus?
options: A history of process management
A review of unrelated documentation tools
A summary of HR policy
Building checklists, decision-history templates, and a versioned delivery framework extracted from the engagements you actually ran
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches how a practice stops depending on one person remembering everything by building and versioning repeatable assets.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: Design the framework from a textbook so it is complete and correct
A checklist is a to-do list that restates the work you already planned
A checklist names the silent, expensive step that has actually failed, and a template field carries the reasoning a past engagement learned
Build the framework as the final version so it never changes
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a checklist is a pre-mortem device and a template is a captured decision history, each designed against a real failure.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Never version a framework because it is the final method
A framework without gates is a timeline, and the gate is where a failure becomes cheap and visible
Automate a step before the process is stable to save time
The v1 should be the perfect system built on your first pass
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the gate discipline is what makes delivery repeatable and priceable, and that v1 is the honest first cut.

questions.question: Per the lesson about measuring outcomes and reporting value to the buyer, what is the central focus?
options: Measuring the activity an agent generates, such as sessions, tokens, and run counts
Proving delivery by pointing at a working, stable agent system
Measuring outcomes rather than activity, against a pre-agreed baseline, and reporting value in the buyer's language
Delivering a single large value report at the end of the engagement
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that delivery (you built what you said) is not value (the buyer is better off), so the consultant measures business outcomes against a frozen baseline and reports them in the buyer's units.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on when and how to capture a baseline?
options: Reconstruct the baseline after delivery from the client's memory of the old process
Freeze the baseline in writing, from the client's real data, before the solution exists, so neither side can drift the before-state
Offer a baseline estimate to the client and let them correct it at the end
Use token and session counts as the baseline since they are easy to collect
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that a baseline reconstructed later gets idealized in memory, so the honest consultant records the agreed, data-backed starting number before the solution exists.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Report every metric you can measure so the buyer sees the full picture
Ignore alternative explanations so the agent appears to own all the improvement
Report on your own convenience and deliver the full story in the closing meeting
Name the counterfactual yourself, claim only the share the agent honestly owns, and report on the buyer's rhythm in small honest installments
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that three airtight metrics beat eight with a soft link, that naming the other initiative first preserves credibility, and that repeated small reports build trust better than a single end-of-engagement reveal.

questions.question: Per the lesson about training the client's team to own the system, what is the central focus?
options: Building operational, change, and sustaining ownership so named operators can run, change, and teach the system without you
A history of corporate training methods
Instruction on designing slide decks for workshops
A review of project management software
questions.explanation: The lesson defines ownership as three distinct capabilities (run, change, sustain) and teaches training that builds all three.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance on training versus demonstration?
options: Give a narrated demo so the client watches the system work and feels confident
If you are the one typing, the client is not learning to own it, so keep your hands off the controls and let them do real tasks
Train the whole department at once so everyone gets the overview
Training is the same thing as handing over the operating docs and runbooks
questions.explanation: The lesson's rule is that a training session has the client run the system, read the output, make mistakes, and figure things out while you coach, and never a demo where you carry the work.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support about sustaining the capability over time?
options: Train one highly capable operator and the team is fully self-sufficient
Escalation is a sign of weakness, so operators should improvise on judgment calls
An operator should trust a plausible-looking output over a stated standard such as the golden set
Name at least two operators and train the trainer, so no single person's absence stops the work and the capability survives the first turnover before you leave
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches two operators at the same standard plus a train-the-trainer step, verified by watching the team teach a new member without you, so ownership survives any single person leaving.

questions.question: For the Linehaul engagement, why is the duplicate-lane cleanup best treated as an exclusion rather than absorbed into the build?
options: Cleaning the spreadsheet is faster than building the matching logic, so folding it in cuts the schedule
The duplicates are a data governance problem that predates the project, so the system must be correct on clear rows and loud on ambiguous ones rather than inheriting the cleanup
Deleting the duplicate rows improves the golden set but has no effect on the matching behavior
The rate director prefers the duplicates stay so the spreadsheet stays the single source of truth
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that the duplicates are a client-owned data governance problem you name with evidence and refuse to own, pricing around it: the system must be correct on clear rows and loud on ambiguous ones. This makes the exclusion load-bearing rather than optional.

questions.question: Where does the lesson say buffers belong in the plan, and why?
options: One large buffer at the final week so the estimate has room at the very end
At the end of the calendar only, to absorb any overdue work in a single recovery zone
In small, positioned amounts where uncertainty actually lives, such as after the extract-schema spike, after the first golden-set evaluation, and before handover
Distributed evenly across all eight weeks regardless of risk
questions.explanation: The lesson argues that a single end-of-plan buffer moves all risk to the final week, where it cannot be recovered, so the intermediate habit is small buffers placed at the points of real uncertainty.

questions.question: Which property makes the scope, plan, and estimate a single composed artifact rather than three separate documents?
options: Each phase covers one lifecycle phase and each document uses the same clients

Each artifact strengthens the others: scope provides the testable gates the plan schedules, the plan places buffers where the estimate's risks live, and the estimate names the assumptions the scope survives
All three are written on the same day before any discovery happens
Each document has an equal word count and a corresponding endnote
questions.explanation: The lesson's composition test is interdependence: if you can delete one artifact without weakening the other two, they are stacked, not composed. Scope feeds the plan's gates, the plan prices the estimate, and the estimate names the assumptions scope must survive.
